analysis.one_liner: Ends mandatory immigrant detention, bans for-profit detention centers, and decriminalizes border crossings.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 33 Democratic cosponsors, H.R. 2374 never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul immigration enforcement: end automatic detention for many immigrants, require a custody hearing within 72 hours with a presumption of release, phase out privately run detention centers within three years, repeal criminal penalties for crossing or re-entering the border, strip nearly all crime-related grounds for deportation, and let people deported since 1996 ask to return if their case would come out differently under the new rules. It never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants facing detention and deportation, asylum seekers (who could no longer be mandatorily detained), families of people removed from the country (who could petition to have cases reopened), and immigrant communities subjected to race- or language-based questioning by federal officers. Immigration judges would regain discretion to stop removals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Immigrants facing detention or deportation, and their families

how_it_helps.text: Ends mandatory detention: DHS must make an initial custody decision within 48 hours, a judge must hold a hearing within 72 hours of a challenge, and there is a presumption that the person be released, with detention conditions reviewed monthly.
Bans new or extended contracts with for-profit detention facilities, terminates existing ones within three years, and requires that detention facilities be owned and operated by DHS itself.

Prohibits immigration officers from questioning someone about their status based on race, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, spoken language, or English proficiency, and requires probable cause plus a judge's hearing within 48 hours for warrantless arrests.
Repeals the criminal statutes for improper entry and re-entry, removing federal convictions that currently follow migrants for life and fuel repeat-prosecution programs.

Restores judicial discretion: immigration judges may grant relief from removal for humanitarian reasons, family unity, or the public interest even when a prior conviction would otherwise bar it, and bars state and local police from performing federal immigration enforcement functions or entering immigration data into the national crime database.

Creates a right to come home: people ordered removed or deported since April 1996 whose cases would come out differently under this bill could have their proceedings reopened, with government-paid transportation back to the United States.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit detention contractors lose their detention and monitoring contracts. Taxpayers fund the transition to DHS-owned facilities, a new community-based case management program (with fees to participants banned), and transportation for people returning under the case-reopening provision. Opponents would add that communities bear whatever public-safety risk comes from narrower deportation grounds and shorter detention.

drawbacks.text: The bill strips nearly all crime-related grounds of inadmissibility and deportability and redefines 'aggravated felony' to require a felony with a sentence of at least five years, so people convicted of serious crimes could no longer be deported on those grounds. This is the provision most likely to alarm a majority of lawmakers and is the strongest good-faith objection to the bill.
It imposes a five-year time limit on crime-based removal proceedings against people previously admitted to the United States, and applies retroactively to proceedings already under way.

The right-to-return provision obligates the Attorney General to reopen the cases of anyone deported since April 1996 whose case would differ under the bill, at government expense, an open-ended retroactive commitment that critics called unworkable in scale.

Detention would shift to DHS-owned facilities within three years, a costly build-out for taxpayers, and community case management would also be publicly funded, though likely cheaper than bed-based detention.

The government would bear the burden of proving by clear and convincing evidence that detention is justified, a high bar that opponents argue makes it harder to hold people who pose a real public-safety risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The detention reforms and decriminalization provisions are where the benefits to ordinary families are clearest and the fiscal trade-off is manageable: community supervision costs far less per person than a detention bed, and repealing entry crimes spares people lifelong felony records. But the bill was drafted to go well beyond that, wiping out nearly all crime-based deportation grounds and reopening every removal case since 1996, which is why it drew no Republican support and never moved. An honest reading is that the bill bundled genuinely popular detention reforms with the broadest possible rollback of criminal-based removal, and its sponsors never narrowed it to the parts that could pass.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress without ever getting a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, so it expired in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia of Illinois introduced the New Way Forward Act on March 29, 2023, with 33 Democratic cosponsors joining him.
That same day the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, and the public record shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote.
The Judiciary Committee was chaired by a Republican, and with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill never reached the floor for a vote in either 2023 or 2024.

When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill died with it; every provision — the detention limits, the private-prison ban, the repeal of entry crimes — expired without ever being tested in a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing immigration enforcement system and the for-profit detention industry: because the bill never advanced, private detention contracts, mandatory detention, and criminal prosecution of border crossings all remained in place unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private detention companies and the enforcement status quo

for.name: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, the flagship immigration-enforcement reform of the House Progressive Caucus wing.

for.name: 33 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Representatives Casar, Pressley, Ocasio-Cortez, Tlaib, Omar, and McGovern.

for.name: Immigrant-rights and civil-liberties advocacy groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed the New Way Forward framework's detention and decriminalization goals.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat at referral for the entire Congress with no committee action.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor in the two years it was pending.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 34 of 216 House Democrats — no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee took no action on it.

industries.industry: Private prison and immigrant detention contractors
industries.note: The bill bans new or extended for-profit detention contracts and terminates existing ones within three years, requiring detention to shift to government-run facilities. This would eliminate the core revenue stream of the private immigrant detention business; nothing in the record suggests the industry opposed this bill, but its interest ran squarely against the bill's main effect.

The community-based alternatives program may not use ankle monitors or other electronic surveillance, cutting these firms out of the alternative-to-detention market, which the bill redirects to nonprofit community organizations.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: State and local officers would be barred from performing federal immigration enforcement, and immigration status would be purged from the national crime database. Agencies participating in 287(g) agreements would lose that role.
With a presumption of release and a requirement that judges consider a person's ability to pay before setting bond, both detention stays and bond transactions would shrink.
